title: The Impact of PERMA Model-Based Positive Psychological Intervention on Preoperative Anxiety in Young Female Patients with Lung Cancer Undergoing Day Surgery
abstract: To assess the efficacy and clinical value of a PERMA model-based positive psychological intervention for reducing preoperative anxiety and enhancing psychological outcomes in young female lung cancer patients undergoing day surgery. This randomized controlled trial included 144 female patients aged 18–40 years with lung cancer scheduled for day surgery between March and June 2025. Patients were assigned to receive either PERMA-based intervention plus routine care (n =73) or routine care alone (n = 71). The primary outcome was preoperative anxiety measured by the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS). Secondary outcomes included depression, stigma, fear of cancer recurrence, fertility concerns, quality of life, social integration, health education acceptance, ERAS execution rates, and patient satisfaction. Between-group differences were analyzed using mean differences with 95% confidence intervals and Cohen’s d; secondary outcomes were adjusted using the Holm-Bonferroni method. Baseline characteristics were well-balanced between groups. After intervention, the intervention group had significantly lower anxiety, depression, stigma, and fear of cancer recurrence than the control group (all p 0.001). The intervention group also achieved higher scores for quality of life, subjective well-being, and social integration, along with reduced fertility concerns (all p 0.05). Most secondary outcomes remained significant after Holm-Bonferroni adjustment. The PERMA model-based positive psychological intervention significantly and meaningfully reduces preoperative anxiety, while improving psychological well-being, quality of life, social integration, and perioperative engagement in young female lung cancer patients undergoing day surgery. It is suitable for integration into perioperative care for this vulnerable population.
